ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure is a regular five-pointed star, and the five outer tips constitute the five vertices of a regular pentagon. Angle α is marked at the right outer tip, formed by the nearly horizontal star-shaped segment from that right tip to the left and the slanted segment from that right tip to the lower left; it is an acute angle. Reasoning: Let the right outer tip be B, and the two star-shaped segments that form α connect respectively to two other outer tips D and E. For a regular five-pointed star, these five outer tips lie equally spaced on the same circle, that is, they are the vertices of a regular pentagon. D and E are adjacent vertices in the regular pentagon, so their corresponding central angle is 360°/5 = 72°. Angle α is an inscribed angle, and it subtends the arc between adjacent vertices D and E, therefore α = 72°/2 = 36°.

raw_record.question_text: How big is the angle $\alpha$ in the regular five-sided star shown?

method.method_draft: First inspect the diagram: it is a regular five-point star, and α is the acute angle at the right outer tip, formed by the top horizontal star segment and the diagonal segment running down-left from that tip. Use the text statement that the star is regular, so its five outer tips are equally spaced vertices of a regular pentagon on a circle. Label the right tip B and the two star vertices connected to it by the two sides of α as D and E; these two endpoints are adjacent vertices of the underlying regular pentagon. The central angle between adjacent vertices of a regular pentagon is 360°/5 = 72°. Since α is an inscribed angle subtending that adjacent-vertex arc, α = 72°/2 = 36°.
